l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: The narrator prays against the mockers, sets a watch day and night, and posts guards by family groups with swords, spears, and bows. He exhorts the nobles, rulers, and people not to fear, keeps the trumpeter by his side, orders the people to rally to the trumpet, and has everyone lodge in Jerusalem. He and his brothers, servants, and guards do not take off their clothes.

l: adversaries, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites mock the builders and then grow very angry as the breaches are filled. They say the Jews will not see them coming until they are among them to kill them and stop the work, but they learn that their plan is known and that God has frustrated it.

l: builders and burden bearers, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: The builders and burden bearers work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other, and each builder wears his sword at his side. Half the people hold spears from morning until the stars appear, and they are told to rally to the sound of the trumpet because they are spread far apart on the wall.

l: conspiracy to attack Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites conspire together to come and fight against Jerusalem and cause confusion. They plan to come among the Jews unseen and kill them to stop the work, but the plot is met with prayer, a watch, armed guards, and is brought to nothing when the enemies learn their plan is known.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 describes a great cry from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews, who were mortgaging fields, vineyards, and houses to buy grain during famine and to pay the king's tribute, and who were bringing sons and daughters into bondage. The narrator, whose speech is in the first person, became very angry, consulted with himself, and confronted the nobles and rulers for exacting usury from their brothers. He held a great assembly against them, reminded them that he had redeemed Jews sold to the nations, and urged them to stop the usury and restore the fields, vineyards, olive groves, houses, and the hundredth part they had charged. The nobles and rulers agreed, took an oath before the priests, and the assembly said Amen and praised the LORD after he shook out his lap as a sign of what would befall anyone who broke the promise. He then recounts that during his twelve years as governor, from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, he did not take the governor's food allowance, unlike former governors, and fed one hundred fifty men at his table, and he closes by asking God to remember him for his good.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: Nehemiah, angered by the people's cry, confronted the nobles and rulers over usury, held a great assembly, and had them promise and swear to restore what they had taken. He did not take the governor's bread during his twelve years as governor from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, because of the fear of God. He worked on the wall, bought no land, hosted one hundred fifty men at his table, and asked God to remember him for the good he had done.

l: the Jews (Nehemiah's brothers), The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: Jews who were poor suffered from famine, mortgaged their fields, vineyards, and houses, borrowed for the king's tribute, and saw their sons and daughters brought into bondage. Nehemiah noted that he and others had redeemed Jews sold to the nations, and he argued that selling them again would be wrong.

l: nobles and rulers, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: The nobles and rulers were accused by Nehemiah of exacting usury from their brothers, and they had no answer when he confronted them in a great assembly. They then promised to restore the property and the charges taken and to require nothing more, and they took an oath before the priests.

l: the people, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: The people, together with their wives, raised a great cry about their hardship, saying they had mortgaged their land for grain and for the king's tribute and that their children were in bondage. After the nobles' promise, all the assembly said Amen and praised the LORD, and the people did according to the promise. Nehemiah also notes that former governors burdened them with bread, wine, and forty shekels of silver, while he did not demand the governor's pay because the bondage was heavy on them.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: God is invoked as the reason to walk in fear, so as to avoid the reproach of the nations, and Nehemiah says he did not burden the people because of the fear of God. The assembly praised the LORD, and Nehemiah's gesture of shaking out his lap called on God to shake out anyone who broke the promise. Nehemiah closes by asking God to remember him for his good.

l: usury, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: Usury was being exacted by the nobles and rulers from their own brothers, and Nehemiah condemned it as not good. He asked that it stop and that the hundredth part of money, grain, new wine, and oil being charged be restored, and the nobles agreed.

l: debt bondage, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: Debt bondage is shown in the people's complaint that they were bringing their sons and daughters into servitude, and some daughters were already in bondage, because others held their fields and vineyards. Nehemiah contrasts this with having redeemed Jews sold to the nations, and he says the bondage was heavy on the people.

l: mortgaged property (fields, vineyards, houses), The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 5
s: Fields, vineyards, and houses were mortgaged to get grain during the famine and to pay the king's tribute, and other men came to hold them. Nehemiah demanded that the fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses be restored that very day, and the nobles and rulers promised to do so.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: Nehemiah's enemies Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem the Arabian learn that the wall is built with no breach left, though the gates have no doors yet. Sanballat and Geshem four times invite Nehemiah to meet them in the plain of Ono, intending harm, and Nehemiah refuses each time, saying he is doing a great work. Sanballat then sends an open letter accusing Nehemiah of plotting rebellion and kingship, which Nehemiah denies as invention, and the hired Shemaiah urges him to hide in the temple, which Nehemiah refuses, discerning that God had not sent him. The wall is finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul in fifty-two days, and the surrounding nations lose confidence, perceiving the work was done by God. Meanwhile nobles of Judah, bound to Tobiah by oath and marriage ties, exchange letters with him and report Nehemiah's words to him, and Tobiah sends letters to put Nehemiah in fear.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: Nehemiah refuses four invitations to meet at Ono, saying he is doing a great work and cannot come down. He denies the accusation in Sanballat's open letter and rejects Shemaiah's advice to hide in the temple, discerning that God had not sent him. He prays that God remember Tobiah, Sanballat, Noadiah and the other prophets, and the wall is completed under his leadership in fifty-two days.

l: Sanballat the Horonite, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: Sanballat, with Geshem, sends to Nehemiah four times inviting him to Ono with intent to harm him. The fifth time he sends a servant with an open letter accusing Nehemiah of planning rebellion and kingship. He and Tobiah had hired Shemaiah to frighten Nehemiah, and Nehemiah asks God to remember him for these works.

l: Tobiah the Ammonite, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: Tobiah is among the enemies who hear the wall is built and, with Sanballat, hires Shemaiah to frighten Nehemiah into sin. Many in Judah are sworn to him, since he is son-in-law of Shecaniah and his son Jehohanan married Meshullam's daughter. Nobles of Judah exchange letters with him, praise his good deeds to Nehemiah, and report Nehemiah's words to him, while he sends letters to put Nehemiah in fear.

l: Geshem the Arabian, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: Geshem the Arabian is named among the enemies who hear that the wall is built. He joins Sanballat in sending to Nehemiah to propose a meeting in the plain of Ono, though they intended to harm him.

l: wall of Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: The wall is reported to be built with no breach left, though the doors have not yet been set in the gates. It is finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days. Its completion frightens the surrounding nations, who perceive it was accomplished by God.

l: enemies (Nehemiah's enemies), The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: Nehemiah's enemies try to lure him to Ono, accuse him of rebellion, and hire a prophet to frighten him, all to weaken the work. When the wall is finished, the surrounding nations are afraid and lose their confidence, perceiving the work was done by God.

l: Sanballat's open letter, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: Sanballat's servant delivers this open letter the fifth time, reporting among the nations and from Gashmu that Nehemiah and the Jews intend to rebel and that he would be king. It claims Nehemiah has appointed prophets to proclaim a king in Judah, threatens that the king will be told, and calls for a meeting to take counsel. Nehemiah answers that no such things are done and that Sanballat imagines them from his own heart.

l: Shemaiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: Shemaiah, son of Delaiah son of Mehetabel, is shut in at his home when Nehemiah visits him. He urges Nehemiah to meet in the temple and shut its doors because assassins will come at night. Nehemiah refuses and discerns that God had not sent him and that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: God is the one Nehemiah appeals to, asking Him to remember Tobiah, Sanballat, Noadiah and the other prophets for their works. Nehemiah discerns that God had not sent Shemaiah. The nations perceive that the finished wall was the work of God.

l: plot to intimidate Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 6
s: The plot includes repeated invitations to Ono, an open letter alleging rebellion, and Shemaiah's hired prophecy urging Nehemiah into the temple so that he would sin and give enemies material for an evil report. Nehemiah rejects each element. Tobiah's letters to put him in fear continue even after the wall is finished.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: After the wall is finished and the doors, gatekeepers, singers, and Levites are in place, the narrator puts his brother Hanani and Hananiah, governor of the fortress, in charge of Jerusalem and gives orders about when the gates are opened and shut and how watches are kept. The city is wide and large but has few people and unbuilt houses, so God moves the narrator to gather the nobles, rulers, and people to be listed by genealogy. He finds the book of the genealogy of those who first came up from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others, and the chapter reproduces its lists by family and town, then priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and Solomon's servants. Some families, including three priestly houses, could not prove their ancestry and the priests among them were disqualified from the priesthood until a priest could consult Urim and Thummim. The assembly totals forty-two thousand three hundred sixty, plus servants, singers, and animals, and the governor, heads of households, and the rest of the people give gold, silver, basins, and priests' garments to the work before everyone settles in their cities in the seventh month.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: As narrator, he appoints his brother Hanani and Hananiah to govern Jerusalem and instructs them on opening, closing, and guarding the gates. Moved by God, he gathers the nobles, rulers, and people to be listed by genealogy and finds the book of the genealogy of the first returnees.

l: Hanani, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: Hanani, the narrator's brother, is put in charge of Jerusalem together with Hananiah. He is to see that the gates stay shut until the sun is hot and that watches are kept.

l: Hananiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: Hananiah, governor of the fortress, is put in charge of Jerusalem alongside Hanani. He is described as a faithful man who feared God above many.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: Jerusalem has its wall built and doors set up, with gatekeepers, singers, and Levites appointed. The city is wide and large but sparsely populated, with houses not yet built, and its gates are to be opened only when the sun is hot and guarded by watches of its inhabitants.

l: book of the genealogy, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: The narrator finds this book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first, and the chapter copies its contents. It lists the returnees by family and town, along with priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and Solomon's servants, and gives a total count.

l: Israel, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: The returnees are the children of the province who came out of captivity under Nebuchadnezzar's deportation and returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own city, with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others. The assembly totals forty-two thousand three hundred sixty, plus male and female servants, singers, horses, mules, camels, and donkeys, and they settle in their cities by the seventh month.

l: temple servants, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: The temple servants are listed by many family names, from Ziha through Hatipha. Together with the children of Solomon's servants they number three hundred ninety-two, and they live in their cities with the rest of Israel.

l: unregistered families, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: People who came up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer could not show their fathers' houses or offspring to prove whether they were of Israel. The children of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda among them number six hundred forty-two.

l: disqualified priests, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: The children of Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, the last named after a Gileadite Barzillai whose daughter their ancestor married, searched for their genealogical records and could not find them. They were deemed disqualified and removed from the priesthood, and the governor told them not to eat the most holy things until a priest could minister with Urim and Thummim.

l: gifts for the work, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: The governor gave one thousand darics of gold, fifty basins, and five hundred thirty priests' garments to the treasury. Some heads of fathers' households gave twenty thousand darics of gold and two thousand two hundred minas of silver, and the rest of the people gave twenty thousand darics of gold, two thousand minas of silver, and sixty-seven priests' garments.

l: genealogical registration of the returnees, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 7
s: God puts it in the narrator's heart to gather the people to be listed by genealogy, and he uses the found genealogy book as the basis. Registration determines status: families who could not prove their lineage were set aside, and priests without records were removed from the priesthood.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: On the first day of the seventh month, all the people gathered in the wide place before the water gate and asked Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses. Ezra read it from early morning until midday while the Levites helped the people understand it, and the people wept when they heard it. Nehemiah the governor, Ezra, and the Levites told them not to mourn because the day was holy and the joy of the LORD was their strength, so the people went to eat, drink, send portions, and celebrate. On the second day the heads of households, priests, and Levites studied the law with Ezra and found the command to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month. The people then built temporary shelters in many places and lived in them with very great gladness, as had not been done since the days of Joshua, and the reading continued daily through the seven-day feast and the solemn assembly on the eighth day.

l: Ezra, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: Ezra the scribe and priest brought the law before the assembly and read it from early morning until midday, standing on a wooden pulpit. He opened the book in sight of all the people and blessed the LORD, and he later met with the household heads, priests, and Levites to study the law. He read from the book daily through the feast.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: Nehemiah, identified as the governor, joined Ezra and the Levites in telling the people not to mourn or weep because the day was holy to the LORD. His role here is as one of the leaders comforting the people after the reading.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: The people gathered as one man, stood when the book was opened, answered "Amen, Amen" with lifted hands, bowed in worship, and wept at hearing the law. They were then told to celebrate, went to eat, drink, and send portions, and later built and lived in temporary shelters, which Israel had not done since the days of Joshua the son of Nun.

l: Levites, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: The Levites, along with named men such as Jeshua, Bani, and Sherebiah, caused the people to understand the law by reading distinctly and giving the sense. They calmed the people, telling them to hold their peace because the day was holy, and were among those who studied the law with Ezra on the second day.

l: book of the law of Moses, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: The people asked Ezra to bring the book, which the LORD had commanded to Israel, and it was read publicly and attentively. Studying it on the second day, the leaders found the command that Israel should dwell in booths in the feast of the seventh month, and it was read day by day through the feast.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: The LORD is the one who commanded Israel through Moses, and Ezra blessed him as the great God while the people worshiped. The day of the reading was declared holy to him, and his joy is described as the people's strength.

l: wide place in front of the water gate, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: This was the open space where all the people gathered and where Ezra read the law from early morning until midday. It was also one of the places where people later built temporary shelters.

l: public reading of the law, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: Ezra read the law aloud to men, women, and all who could understand, on the first day of the seventh month, and the people listened attentively. The Levites explained it so the people understood, and the reading brought weeping, then celebration because they understood the words. Reading continued daily through the feast.

l: Feast of Booths, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: The leaders found in the law the command to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month and to proclaim it in all cities and Jerusalem. The people kept the feast seven days, with a solemn assembly on the eighth day according to the ordinance, and there was very great gladness.

l: temporary shelters (booths), The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8
s: The people gathered olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other thick-tree branches to make temporary shelters. They built them on rooftops, in courts, in the courts of God's house, and in the wide places of the water gate and Ephraim's gate, and the returned exiles lived in them.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: On the twenty-fourth day of the month, the children of Israel gather with fasting, sackcloth, and dirt on them, separate themselves from all foreigners, and confess their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. They read the book of the law for a fourth of the day and confess and worship for another fourth. Levites including Jeshua, Bani, and Kadmiel cry out to the LORD and lead a long prayer that blesses him as creator, recalls his choosing of Abram, his rescue of the people from Egypt, his giving of the law at Sinai, and his provision in the wilderness and in the land. The prayer recounts the repeated pride, rebellion, and disobedience of the fathers, and the LORD's repeated mercy, deliverance, and refusal to make a full end of them. It ends with the confession that the people are servants in the land, under kings set over them because of their sins, and that they make a sure covenant, write it, and have their princes, Levites, and priests seal it.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: The LORD is blessed by the Levites as the one alone who made heaven, earth, and seas and preserves them all. He chose Abram, delivered the people from Egypt, gave the law at Sinai, sustained them in the wilderness, and gave them the land. He repeatedly pardoned and delivered a rebellious people, though he also gave them into the hands of adversaries, and is declared just in all that has come on them.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: The children of Israel assemble with fasting, sackcloth, and dirt, separate from all foreigners, and confess their sins and their fathers' iniquities. They hear the law read, worship, and conclude by acknowledging they are servants in their own land under kings who have power over their bodies and livestock. They make a sure covenant and write it.

l: Levites, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: Levites named Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Chenani, Hashabneiah, Hodiah, and Pethahiah stand on the stairs and cry out loudly to the LORD. They call the people to stand and bless the LORD and lead the long prayer of praise and confession. Their number joins the princes and priests in sealing the covenant.

l: Abraham, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: Abraham, first called Abram, is described as the one the LORD chose and brought out of Ur of the Chaldees, and to whom he gave the name Abraham. The LORD found his heart faithful and made a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Jebusite, and Girgashite to his offspring.

l: Israel, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: The fathers saw affliction in Egypt, were rescued through the sea, led by cloud and fire, and sustained in the wilderness. They behaved proudly, hardened their necks, made a molded calf, killed prophets, and ignored the commandments, so they were given into the hands of adversaries. Yet the LORD did not make a full end of them or forsake them.

l: commandments, statutes and ordinances, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: The LORD gave right ordinances, true laws, statutes, and commandments at Sinai, and made known the holy Sabbath through Moses his servant. The people's ancestors refused to obey them and cast the law behind their backs, though the law is described as one by which a person who does it shall live. In this unit the law is also read aloud to the assembly.

l: land of Canaan, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: The land of the Canaanite and other peoples was promised to Abraham's offspring and later possessed when the LORD subdued its inhabitants before them. It held fortified cities, houses full of good things, cisterns, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees. Now its abundant yield goes to the kings set over the people because of their sins.

l: sure covenant, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: The people declare at the end of the prayer that they make a sure covenant and write it. Their princes, Levites, and priests seal it. It is their response to the confession of their sins and of the LORD's justice.

l: assembly with fasting and confession, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 9
s: On the twenty-fourth day of the month the people gather in sackcloth with dirt on them, separated from all foreigners. They stand, read the law for a fourth of the day, and confess and worship for another fourth. The Levites then lead the prayer that recounts the LORD's works and the people's failures.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: Chapter 10 lists those who sealed the covenant: Nehemiah the governor, a group of priests, the Levites, and the chiefs of the people. The rest of the people, including priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and their families, joined them in a curse and an oath to walk in God's law given by Moses. They pledged not to intermarry with the peoples of the land, not to buy goods on the Sabbath or holy days, and to forego the seventh year crops and the exaction of every debt. They also committed to a yearly third-of-a-shekel charge for the temple service and to supplying wood, first fruits, firstborn, and tithes. The chapter ends with the resolve, 'We will not forsake the house of our God.'

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: Nehemiah, identified as the governor and son of Hacaliah, is the first named among those who sealed the covenant. He appears at the head of the list before the priests, Levites, and chiefs.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: God is the one to whom the oath is made and whose law, given through Moses his servant, the people vow to follow. He is called the LORD our Lord, and his commandments, ordinances, and statutes are to be observed. His house is the object of the people's resolve not to forsake it.

l: priests, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: Twenty-one priests are named among the sealers, beginning after Nehemiah and Zedekiah. They are to receive the first fruits of dough, wave offerings, new wine, and oil at the rooms of the house of God. A priest descended from Aaron is to be with the Levites when they take tithes, and priests who minister are among those served by the rooms where the vessels are kept.

l: Levites, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: The Levites sealed the covenant, with Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui, Kadmiel, and their brothers named. They receive the tithes of the ground in the farming villages and must bring up the tithe of the tithes to the treasure house in the house of God. They also took part in casting lots for the wood offering.

l: Israel, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: The chiefs of the people are listed by name as sealers, and the rest of the people, with wives, sons, and daughters, who had knowledge and understanding, joined in the oath. They commit to marriage restrictions, Sabbath and seventh-year observance, a yearly third-shekel charge, wood offerings by lot, and bringing first fruits, firstborn, and tithes. They declare they will not forsake the house of their God.

l: peoples of the lands, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: The peoples of the lands are those from whom the covenanting people had separated themselves to follow the law of God. The people vow not to give their daughters to them or take their daughters for their sons. They also vow not to buy wares or grain from them on the Sabbath or a holy day.

l: oath and curse (covenant), The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: The people, joined with their brothers and nobles, entered into a curse and an oath to walk in God's law and keep all the LORD's commandments, ordinances, and statutes. Its specific terms include no intermarriage, Sabbath trade restrictions, forgoing the seventh year crops and debt exaction, supporting the temple, and bringing offerings and tithes. Leaders sealed it by name.

l: law of God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: The law of God was given by Moses the servant of God, and the people bind themselves by oath to walk in it. It is cited as the basis for the wood offering and for the firstborn of sons, livestock, herds, and flocks being brought to the house of God.

l: God's house, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: The house of God is the focus of the covenant's financial and ritual provisions: the yearly third-shekel charge supports its service, including the show bread, offerings, Sabbaths, feasts, and sin offerings. Wood, first fruits, firstborn, and tithes are brought to it, with rooms and a treasure house storing them. The chapter closes with the vow, 'We will not forsake the house of our God.'

l: first fruits and tithes, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 10
s: The people pledge to bring the first fruits of the ground and of all kinds of trees, the firstborn of sons and livestock, and the first fruits of dough, wave offerings, new wine, and oil to the priests at the house of God. The tithes of the ground go to the Levites in the farming villages, and the Levites bring the tithe of the tithes to the treasure house. The offerings are brought to the rooms where the vessels of the sanctuary are.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: Chapter 11 describes who settled in Jerusalem, the holy city. The princes of the people lived there, and the rest of the people cast lots so that one in ten would dwell in Jerusalem while nine parts stayed in the other cities; the people blessed those who volunteered. The chapter lists the chiefs from Judah (including Athaiah and Maaseiah) and Benjamin (including Sallu), the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, and the singers, with their numbers and overseers. The temple servants lived in Ophel, and the rest of Israel, the priests, and the Levites lived in their own cities. Finally the chapter names the villages where the children of Judah lived from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom and where the children of Benjamin lived from Geba onward, noting that some Levite divisions of Judah settled in Benjamin's territory.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: Jerusalem, called the holy city, was settled by the princes of the people and by one in ten of the rest, chosen by lot. Its residents included 468 sons of Perez, 928 Benjamites, priests, 284 Levites, and 172 gatekeepers.

l: princes of the people, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: The princes of the people lived in Jerusalem.

l: people (people of the province), The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: The rest of the people cast lots to bring one in ten to live in Jerusalem, with nine parts staying in the other cities. They blessed all the men who willingly offered themselves to dwell in Jerusalem.

l: cities of Judah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: In the cities of Judah, everyone lived on his own possession: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the children of Solomon's servants. The residue of Israel, the priests, and the Levites lived there, each in his inheritance.

l: priests, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: Priests who lived in Jerusalem included Jedaiah, Jachin, Seraiah (ruler of God's house), Adaiah, and Amashsai, with brothers numbering 822, 242, and 128. Their overseer was Zabdiel, and other priests remained in the cities of Judah.

l: Levites, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: The Levites in Jerusalem numbered 284, with leaders including Shemaiah, Shabbethai, Jozabad, Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, and Abda. Uzzi of the sons of Asaph oversaw them, and the singers had a settled provision by the king's commandment. Some Levite divisions of Judah settled in Benjamin's territory.

l: Judah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: Some children of Judah lived in Jerusalem, among them Athaiah and Maaseiah, and 468 valiant sons of Perez. Others lived in villages and towns from Kiriath Arba and Beersheba to Azekah, encamping from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom.

l: children of Benjamin, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: Some children of Benjamin lived in Jerusalem, led by Sallu, with Gabbai and Sallai and 928 men in all; Joel the son of Zichri was their overseer and Judah the son of Hassenuah was second over the city. Others lived from Geba onward in places such as Michmash, Bethel, Anathoth, Nob, Lod, and Ono.

l: lots casting, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 11
s: The people cast lots to determine which one of every ten would dwell in Jerusalem, the holy city. The other nine parts lived in the other cities.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: Chapter 12 lists the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, the high priestly line from Jeshua to Jaddua, and the heads of priestly households in the days of Joiakim. It records the Levite chiefs, singers, and gatekeepers who served according to David's commandment. The narrator (Nehemiah) then describes the dedication of Jerusalem's wall, for which Levites and singers were gathered, and the priests, Levites, people, gates, and wall were purified. Two great thanksgiving companies processed along the wall in opposite directions and met at God's house, where sacrifices were offered and the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away. The chapter ends with men appointed over the storerooms for offerings and tithes and a note that the portions for singers, gatekeepers, and Levites were given as each day required.

l: priests, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: The priests who went up with Zerubbabel and Jeshua are listed by name, along with the heads of their fathers' households in the days of Joiakim. At the dedication they purified themselves, and priests' sons blew trumpets in the procession and stood with trumpets in God's house. Judah rejoiced for the priests and Levites who served, and the Levites set apart a portion for the sons of Aaron.

l: Levites, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: The Levites who returned include Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, who was over the thanksgiving songs. Their chiefs praised and gave thanks according to David's commandment, and some served as gatekeepers at the storehouses. They were sought out from all their places to come to Jerusalem for the dedication, purified themselves and the people, and received portions that Israel gave and set apart.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: Nehemiah is named as governor in whose days the Levites and priests served, alongside Ezra the priest and scribe. Speaking in the first person, he brought the princes of Judah up on the wall, appointed the two great thanksgiving companies, and followed the second company with half of the people. He stood in God's house with half of the rulers after the processions.

l: singers, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: The sons of the singers gathered from the plain around Jerusalem and from villages of the Netophathites, Beth Gilgal, and the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, where they had built villages around Jerusalem. At the dedication they sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah. Their portions were given by all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, according to the commandment of David and Solomon.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: Jerusalem is where the Levites were brought together for the dedication, and the singers had built villages around it. Its joy over the great sacrifices, with women and children rejoicing, was heard far away. Men were also appointed there over the rooms for treasures, offerings, first fruits, and tithes.

l: wall of Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: The wall was purified by the priests and Levites before the dedication. The princes of Judah and the two thanksgiving companies went up on it, passing gates and towers including the dung gate, spring gate, water gate, gate of Ephraim, old gate, fish gate, sheep gate, tower of the furnaces, tower of Hananel, and tower of Hammeah, ending at the gate of the guard.

l: dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: The dedication was held with gladness, thanksgiving, and singing with cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps. Levites and singers were gathered to Jerusalem, and the priests, Levites, people, gates, and wall were purified first. It included processions, great sacrifices, and rejoicing, and on that day men were appointed over the storerooms.

l: two thanksgiving companies, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 12
s: Nehemiah appointed two great companies to give thanks and go in procession on the wall. One went to the right toward the dung gate, led by Hoshaiah with half of the princes of Judah, priests with trumpets, and Ezra the scribe before them. The other went to meet them with Nehemiah and half the people, and both companies then stood in God's house.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Nehemiah 13 recounts reforms Nehemiah carried out after returning to Jerusalem from the king. The reading of the law led the people to separate the mixed multitude from Israel, and Nehemiah found that the priest Eliashib had given Tobiah a great room in the temple courts, which he cleared and restored to its storage use. He restored the Levites' neglected portions and appointed treasurers, stopped Sabbath trading by Judeans and Tyrian merchants by shutting the gates, and confronted men who had married foreign women, including a grandson of Eliashib who was son-in-law to Sanballat. Nehemiah repeatedly asks God to remember him for these acts.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem after leave from the king and was grieved to find Tobiah housed in the temple courts, so he threw out Tobiah's belongings and had the rooms cleansed. He restored the Levites' portions, appointed treasurers, shut the gates against Sabbath trade, threatened the merchants, and confronted, cursed, struck and made oaths of men who married foreign women. He closes several times asking God to remember him for good.

l: Eliashib the high priest, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Eliashib, appointed over the rooms of God's house and allied to Tobiah, prepared a great room for Tobiah where the offerings and vessels had been stored. Nehemiah condemned this as evil. A son of Joiada, Eliashib's son, is also named as having married into Sanballat's family.

l: Tobiah the Ammonite, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Tobiah was given a great room in the temple courts by his ally Eliashib the priest. When Nehemiah returned, he threw all of Tobiah's household stuff out of the room.

l: room (Tobiah's room in the temple courts), The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: The great room had previously stored the meal offerings, frankincense, vessels and tithes of grain, new wine and oil, but Eliashib prepared it for Tobiah. Nehemiah had Tobiah's goods thrown out, the rooms cleansed, and the vessels, meal offerings and frankincense brought back in.

l: Israel, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Upon hearing the law, Israel separated all the mixed multitude from itself, in line with the rule excluding Ammonites and Moabites. Nehemiah warned that profaning the Sabbath would bring more wrath on Israel, and recalled that Solomon, king over all Israel, was caused to sin by foreign women.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: God is said to have turned Balaam's curse into a blessing, and is recalled as having brought evil on the people and the city for earlier Sabbath violations. Nehemiah repeatedly asks God to remember him and not wipe out his good deeds, and appeals to God's loving kindness. God also loved Solomon and made him king over all Israel.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem and found the temple room misused and Sabbath trade being carried on in the city. Men of Tyre and others brought goods in on the Sabbath, until Nehemiah had the gates shut at dusk before the Sabbath.

l: God's house, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: The house of God was neglected because the Levites' portions were not given and the workers fled to their fields, and its courts held a room for Tobiah. Nehemiah cleansed the rooms, restored the offerings and vessels, and had the people bring tithes to the treasuries again.

l: Levites, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: The Levites and singers had fled to their fields because their portions were not given. Nehemiah gathered them back to their places, set faithful treasurers to distribute to them, and commanded them to purify themselves and keep the gates to sanctify the Sabbath. Their duties were appointed, each in his work.

l: Judah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: All Judah brought the tithes of grain, new wine and oil to the treasuries once Nehemiah restored order. Some in Judah were treading wine presses and carrying burdens on the Sabbath, and Nehemiah rebuked the nobles of Judah for profaning it.

l: Sabbath, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Nehemiah saw Judeans working and merchants selling on the Sabbath, and rebuked the nobles for profaning it. He had the gates shut at dusk before the Sabbath and kept closed until it ended, posted his servants there, and later had the Levites guard the gates to sanctify the day.

l: goldsmiths and merchants, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Tyrian men living in Jerusalem and other merchants brought fish and wares to sell on the Sabbath. After the gates were shut they camped outside the wall once or twice, until Nehemiah threatened to lay hands on them and they stopped coming on the Sabbath.

l: sheep gate, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Nehemiah commanded that the gates be shut as they grew dark before the Sabbath and not opened until it ended, with his servants set over them. Later the Levites, after purifying themselves, were commanded to keep the gates.

l: Jews who married foreign women, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Nehemiah saw Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, whose children spoke half in the speech of Ashdod and not the Jews' language. He contended with them, cursed them, struck some, plucked out their hair, and made them swear not to intermarry. One son of Joiada, son-in-law to Sanballat, was chased away.

l: intermarriage, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 13
s: Marriage with foreign women is treated as great evil and trespass against God, and Nehemiah cites Solomon, who was caused to sin by foreign women. He made the offenders swear not to give or take daughters in marriage with foreigners, and said such marriages defiled the priesthood and its covenant.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes / Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 of Ecclesiastes introduces the Preacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, who declares that all is vanity. He asks what man gains from his labor under the sun and observes that generations, the sun, the wind, and the rivers move in endless cycles while the earth remains. He states that there is nothing new under the sun and that nothing is remembered of former or later things. The Preacher then recounts applying his heart to seek out all that is done under the sky, finding it a heavy burden and a chasing after wind. He concludes that though he gained great wisdom, knowing wisdom, madness and folly is also a chasing after wind, since much wisdom brings much grief and increased knowledge increases sorrow.

l: the Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes / Chapter 1
s: The Preacher is introduced as the son of David and king over Israel in Jerusalem, who speaks the words of the chapter. He applied his heart to seek out by wisdom all that is done under the sky, saw all the works under the sun, and judged them vanity and a chasing after wind. He claims to have obtained great wisdom above all who were before him in Jerusalem, yet perceived that seeking wisdom, madness and folly was also a chasing after wind.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes / Chapter 1
s: The Preacher declares "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." He repeats the verdict after seeing all the works done under the sun, calling them vanity and a chasing after wind, and says that his pursuit of wisdom, madness and folly was likewise a chasing after wind.

l: human labor, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes / Chapter 1
s: The Preacher asks what man gains from all his labor in which he labors under the sun, implying no clear gain. He describes the work and the search to understand what is done under the sky as a heavy burden that God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with. He says all the works done under the sun are vanity and a chasing after wind.

l: nothing new, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes / Chapter 1
s: The Preacher says that what has been is what shall be, and what has been done is what shall be done, so there is no new thing under the sun. He asks whether anything can be called new and answers that it has been long ago, in the ages before us. He adds that there is no memory of the former things, nor will there be of the latter things among those who come after.

l: wisdom, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes / Chapter 1
s: The Preacher says he applied his heart to seek and search out by wisdom, and that he obtained great wisdom above all who were before him in Jerusalem, with great experience of wisdom and knowledge. He applied his heart to know wisdom, madness and folly, and perceived that this was also a chasing after wind. He concludes that in much wisdom is much grief, and that whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: In Chapter 2 the narrator, a king in Jerusalem, tests mirth and pleasure, then builds great works: houses, vineyards, gardens, pools, servants, herds, silver, gold, and singers. He allows himself every joy, yet concludes that all of it is vanity and a chasing after wind with no profit under the sun. He compares wisdom and folly, finding wisdom better as light is better than darkness, but sees that the wise man and the fool share one fate and are both forgotten. He comes to hate his labor because he must leave it to a successor who may be wise or foolish, and he despairs. He ends by saying that eating, drinking, and enjoying one's labor is from the hand of God, who gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please him and toil to the sinner.

l: the Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: The narrator tests mirth, builds great works, amasses wealth, and withholds no joy from himself, yet judges it all vanity with no profit under the sun. He considers wisdom and folly, hates his life and labor because of death and the successor who will inherit it, and comes to despair. He finally sees that enjoying food, drink, and labor is from God's hand, and asks who can enjoy more than he.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: God is named as the source of the enjoyment a man finds in eating, drinking, and his labor. He gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to the man who pleases him, and gives the sinner the travail of gathering and heaping up so that it may pass to the one who pleases God.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: Vanity, along with a chasing after wind, is the narrator's verdict on mirth, his great works, the lack of profit under the sun, the shared fate of wise and fool, his labor left to a successor, a man's sorrowful days, and God's allotment to the sinner. It is repeated throughout the chapter, and the narrator once calls the inheritance of labor by one who did not work for it also a great evil.

l: wisdom, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: The narrator says wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness, and that his wisdom remained with him through his pursuits. However, he sees that the wise man meets the same event as the fool and is equally forgotten, so he asks why he was more wise and calls this also vanity. God gives wisdom to the man who pleases him.

l: fool (the foolish), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: Folly is something the narrator considers and tries to lay hold of, and the fool is said to walk in darkness. Wisdom excels it, yet the fool shares the wise man's fate and is equally forgotten. The narrator also worries that his successor may be a fool.

l: mirth and pleasure, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: The narrator tests himself with mirth and pleasure, cheering his flesh with wine, and calls laughter foolishness and asks what mirth accomplishes. He withholds his heart from no joy and takes it as his portion from his labor, but concludes this too is vanity. Later he says enjoyment in one's labor is good and from God's hand.

l: great works and possessions (the narrator's), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: The narrator makes houses, vineyards, gardens, parks, fruit trees, and pools, and acquires servants, herds, flocks, silver, gold, the treasure of kings, singers, and musical instruments, surpassing all before him in Jerusalem. On reviewing them he finds all vanity with no profit under the sun. He hates the labor behind them because he must leave it to the man who comes after him.

l: successor (the man who comes after the narrator), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: The successor will rule over all of the narrator's labor, and the narrator does not know whether he will be wise or a fool. The narrator notes that the king's successor can only do what was done long ago, and that a man's labor may be left to one who did not work for it, which he calls vanity and a great evil.

l: death, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 2
s: Death comes to the wise man just as to the fool, and the narrator sees that one event happens to them all. Because of it neither is remembered forever, and the narrator asks why he was more wise. It contributes to his hatred of life and his despair over his labor, which he must leave behind.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 opens with a catalogue of opposite activities, each assigned its own time under heaven, such as birth and death, weeping and laughing, war and peace. The narrator asks what profit a worker gains from labor and reflects that God has given people a burden, made everything beautiful in its time, and set eternity in human hearts without letting them grasp God's whole work. He concludes that the best course is to rejoice, do good, and enjoy food, drink, and labor as God's gift, since God's work is permanent and meant to inspire fear. Observing wickedness in places of justice, he says God will judge the righteous and the wicked, and that God tests people to show they are like animals, sharing one breath, one fate in death, and a return to dust. He closes by saying nothing is better than rejoicing in one's works, because no one can see what will come after.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: God is said to have given people a burden, made everything beautiful in its time, and set eternity in their hearts, though people cannot find out his work from beginning to end. Whatever he does is forever, with nothing added or taken away, so that men fear him. The narrator says God will judge the righteous and the wicked and tests people to show they are like animals.

l: sons of men, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: The sons of men are given a burden by God and cannot fully discover his work, though eternity is set in their hearts. The narrator says it is best for them to rejoice, do good, and enjoy their labor. They are tested by God to see they are like animals, since they share the animals' fate and cannot know what will be after them.

l: animals, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: Animals are compared to the sons of men: what happens to people happens to them, and they die as people die. They have one breath, come from dust and return to dust. The narrator asks who knows whether the spirit of the animal goes downward to the earth.

l: time and seasons, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: The chapter opens by declaring a season and a time for every purpose under heaven, then lists paired opposites such as birth and death, planting and plucking up, and war and peace. God has made everything beautiful in its time, and there is a time for every purpose and work in judgment.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: The narrator calls all vanity when explaining that man has no advantage over the animals, since both share one breath and one fate. This follows his observation that wickedness occupies even places of justice and righteousness.

l: death, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: Death appears among the appointed times, 'a time to be born, and a time to die.' The narrator says as one dies, so the other dies, for people and animals alike. All go to one place, from dust to dust.

l: the Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: The narrator asks what profit comes from labor and says he has seen the burden God gave people. He saw wickedness in the place of justice and righteousness, and said in his heart that God will judge and that God tests people to show they are like animals. He concludes there is nothing better than to rejoice in one's works.

l: enjoyment of life as God’s gift, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 3
s: The narrator questions the profit of labor but affirms that people should rejoice, do good, eat and drink, and enjoy good in all their labor, which is the gift of God. He calls rejoicing in one's works a person's portion, since no one can see what will be after him.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: The speaker observes the oppressions done under the sun, noting the tears of the oppressed who have no comforter while their oppressors hold power, and concludes that the dead, or those never born, are better off than the living. He sees that labor and achievement spring from a neighbor's envy, which is vanity, and contrasts the fool who ruins himself with the value of a quiet handful over two handfuls won through toil. He describes a solitary man with no son or brother whose endless labor never satisfies him, and then praises two companions who reward each other's work, lift each other up, keep warm together, and withstand an attacker, since a threefold cord is not quickly broken. Finally, he says a poor and wise youth is better than an old and foolish king who will not take admonition, even though the youth rose from prison to kingship, and those who come after will not rejoice in him, so this too is vanity.

l: the oppressed, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: The oppressed are seen weeping under the sun with no comforter. Their plight leads the speaker to praise the dead and the unborn above the living.

l: oppressors, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: Oppressors are described as having power on their side. Because they hold that power, the oppressed have no comforter.

l: oppression, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: The speaker returns and sees all the oppressions done under the sun. They move him to judge the dead, and better still those never born who have not seen this evil work, as better off than the living.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: Vanity is applied to labor driven by a neighbor's envy, to the solitary man's endless toil, and to the succession of a popular young king whom later generations will not rejoice in. It is called a striving after wind and a chasing after wind.

l: labor, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: Labor and achievement are said to be the envy of a man's neighbor, which makes them vanity. Better a handful with quietness than two handfuls with labor, and two people together have a good reward for their labor, while the solitary man's labor has no end and does not satisfy him.

l: solitary man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: The solitary man has neither son nor brother, and there is no end to his labor. His eyes are never satisfied with wealth, and he asks for whom he labors and deprives his soul of enjoyment, a miserable business and vanity. He has no one to lift him if he falls and cannot keep warm alone.

l: two companions, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: Two are better than one because they have a good reward for their labor. If one falls the other lifts him, they keep each other warm, and together they can withstand someone who prevails against one alone.

l: companionship, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: Companionship is shown to bring reward, help in falling, warmth, and defense. The text says a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

l: poor and wise youth, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: The poor and wise youth is declared better than an old and foolish king. He came out of prison to be king, though he was born poor even in the kingdom he came to rule. All the living walk with him, the other who succeeded him, yet those who come after will not rejoice in him.

l: old and foolish king, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 4
s: The old and foolish king is judged worse than the poor and wise youth because he no longer knows how to receive admonition.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 begins by advising caution when approaching God's house: listening is better than the sacrifice of fools, words before God should be few, and vows must be paid promptly because God has no pleasure in fools. It then observes that oppression of the poor in a district should not cause surprise, since officials are watched by higher officials, and that the king profits from the field. The speaker turns to wealth, saying that whoever loves silver is never satisfied, that goods increase those who consume them, and that the laboring man sleeps sweetly while the rich man's abundance keeps him awake. He describes as a grievous evil wealth kept to its owner's harm, lost by misfortune, leaving nothing for a son, since the owner leaves as naked as he came and eats in darkness, frustration, sickness and wrath. He concludes that it is good to eat, drink and enjoy one's labor during the life God gives, and that riches with the power to enjoy them are a gift of God who occupies a person with joy of heart.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: God is in heaven while people are on earth, so words before him should be few, and he has no pleasure in fools and may be angered by a rash voice and destroy the work of one's hands. He is the one who gives life, riches, wealth, and the power to eat and enjoy them, which is called his gift. He occupies a person with the joy of the heart.

l: fool (the foolish), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: Fools offer sacrifices without knowing they do evil, and a fool's speech comes with a multitude of words like a dream with many cares. God has no pleasure in fools who defer paying their vows.

l: vow, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: A vow made to God must not be delayed in payment, and what is vowed must be paid. It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

l: speech and words, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: One should not be rash with the mouth or hasty in heart before God, and words should be few. Many words bring vanities like many dreams, and the mouth should not lead one into sin, such as protesting to the messenger that a vow was a mistake.

l: riches and wealth, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: Love of silver and abundance is never satisfied and is called vanity. As goods increase, those who eat them increase, and the owner gains only the sight of them. Wealth kept to its owner's harm perishes by misfortune, and nothing can be carried away at death.

l: rich owner of wealth, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: The rich man cannot sleep because of his abundance, unlike the laboring man. His riches may perish by misfortune, leaving nothing in his hand for a son, and he leaves naked as he came, eating in darkness with frustration, sickness and wrath. If God gives him the power to enjoy his riches, however, that is God's gift.

l: labor, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: The sleep of a laboring man is sweet whether he eats little or much. Labor for the wind brings no profit at the end, but enjoying good in one's labor all the days God gives is called one's portion and something good and proper.

l: enjoyment of life as God’s gift, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 5
s: The speaker sees it as good and proper to eat, drink, and enjoy the good of one's labor during the days of life God gives, which is one's portion. The power to eat of riches, take one's portion, and rejoice in labor is called the gift of God, who keeps the person occupied with joy so that he does not often brood over the days of his life.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 describes an evil the speaker has seen under the sun: a man given riches, wealth, and honor by God who lacks nothing he desires, yet is not given power to enjoy them, so a stranger eats them instead. The speaker then considers a man who fathers a hundred children and lives many years but is not filled with good and has no burial, declaring a stillborn child better off, since it comes in vanity, departs in darkness, and has rest. Even a man living two thousand years without enjoying good goes to the same place as everyone. The chapter observes that human labor is for the mouth yet appetite is never filled, that the wise have no advantage over the fool, that man cannot contend with one mightier, and that no one knows what is good for man in his shadow-like life or what will come after him.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 6
s: God gives one man riches, wealth, and honor so that he lacks nothing he desires, yet gives him no power to eat of it, so an alien eats it. He is also the one who is mightier than man, with whom man cannot contend.

l: man to whom God gives riches (Ecclesiastes 6:2), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 6
s: He is given riches, wealth, and honor and lacks nothing his soul desires. God gives him no power to enjoy them, and an alien eats them instead, which the speaker calls vanity and an evil disease.

l: man who fathers a hundred children, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 6
s: He lives many years and has a hundred children, but his soul is not filled with good and he has no burial. The speaker says a stillborn child is better than he.

l: stillborn child, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 6
s: It comes in vanity, departs in darkness, and its name is covered with darkness. It has not seen or known the sun, and it has more rest than the man with a hundred children.

l: man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 6
s: Man's labor is all for his mouth, yet his appetite is never filled. He cannot contend with one mightier than he, his name was given long ago, and no one can tell him what is good for him or what will come after him. His life is vain and spent like a shadow.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 6
s: Vanity is attached to the unenjoyed riches, to the stillborn child's coming, to the wandering of desire, which is also called a chasing after wind, and to the many words that multiply it. The speaker also calls man's whole life vain and asks what such words profit him.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: Chapter 7 gathers proverbs contrasting wisdom and folly, with the Preacher arguing that the house of mourning, rebuke, patience, and wisdom are better than feasting, fools' laughter, hasty anger, and bribery. He tells readers to consider the work of God, who makes both prosperity and adversity, and observes that a righteous man may perish while a wicked man lives long. He advises against being overly righteous or overly wicked, notes that no righteous person on earth is free of sin, and says people should not heed every word spoken, since they too have cursed others. The Preacher says he tested all this by wisdom but found it far from him, and that what exists is deeply hidden. He reports finding one man among a thousand but no woman, and concludes that God made mankind upright, but they seek many inventions.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: God has made the day of prosperity and the day of adversity side by side, and no one can straighten what he has made crooked. He made mankind upright, and the one who fears him will come out of all extremes, while whoever pleases him escapes the snaring woman.

l: the Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: The Preacher recounts what he has seen in his days of vanity and says he tested everything by wisdom, resolving to be wise, but wisdom remained far from him. He says his soul still seeks what he has not found, reports finding one man among a thousand but no woman, and concludes that God made mankind upright but they seek many inventions.

l: the wise, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the wise welcome rebuke over the song of fools. Extortion can make a wise man foolish, and wisdom gives the wise man more strength than ten rulers in a city.

l: fool (the foolish), Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: The heart of fools is in the house of mirth, and their laughter is compared to the crackling of thorns under a pot. Anger rests in the bosom of fools, and their song is worse to hear than the rebuke of the wise.

l: wisdom, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: Wisdom is as good as an inheritance and is a defense like money, preserving the life of the one who has it. It is a strength greater than ten rulers, yet the Preacher says that when he sought to be wise, it was far from him.

l: house of mourning, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: It is said to be better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, because it is the end of all men and the living should take it to heart. It is where the heart of the wise is found.

l: righteous man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: A righteous man is observed to perish in his righteousness. The Preacher warns against being overly righteous and says there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin.

l: wicked man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: A wicked man is observed to live long in his evildoing. The Preacher advises against being too wicked, asking why one should die before one's time.

l: man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 7
s: Mankind was made upright by God, but people search for many inventions. The text says all are subject to the sin and the cursing of others that the Preacher describes, and that people cannot find out what lies far off and deep.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: Chapter 8 is the narrator's reflection on wisdom, royal authority, and the limits of human understanding. The narrator urges keeping the king's command because of the oath to God, noting that the king does whatever pleases him and that the obedient wise heart knows the proper time and procedure. He observes that no man controls the spirit or the day of death, that one man sometimes has power over another to his hurt, and that the wicked are buried and forgotten. Because sentence against evil is not executed speedily, people's hearts are set to do evil, yet the narrator affirms it will be better for those who fear God and not well for the wicked. He calls it vanity that the righteous and the wicked sometimes receive each other's due, commends mirth (eating, drinking, being joyful), and concludes that man cannot find out the work of God under the sun, however hard he labors or however wise he claims to be.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: God is the one to whom the oath is owed, which is the reason given for keeping the king's command. He has given man the days of his life, and it will be better with those who fear him and not well with the wicked who do not. His work under the sun cannot be found out by man.

l: king, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: The king's word is supreme, and he does whatever pleases him, so that no one can ask him "What are you doing?" The narrator advises not hastily leaving his presence and keeping his command.

l: the wise, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: The wise man's wisdom makes his face shine and changes its hardness. His wise heart knows the time and procedure, yet even if he thinks he can comprehend the work done under the sun, he will not be able to find it.

l: wicked, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: The wicked are seen buried and forgotten in the city where they acted, though they once came from holiness. A sinner may commit crimes a hundred times and live long, but it will not be well with the wicked, and they will not lengthen their days like a shadow because they do not fear God. Some wicked men receive what the work of the righteous deserves, which the narrator calls vanity.

l: righteous man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: Some righteous men experience what would befit the work of the wicked. The narrator names this a vanity done on the earth.

l: those who fear God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: The narrator knows surely that it will be better with those who fear God and are reverent before him, even when sinners live long in their crimes.

l: sons of men, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: Man's misery is heavy on him, he does not know what will be, and he has no power over the spirit or the day of death. Hearts of the sons of men are set to do evil because sentence is not executed speedily. Man cannot find out the work done under the sun however much he labors, and has no better thing than to eat, drink, and be joyful.

l: king's command, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: The narrator says to keep the king's command because of the oath to God. Whoever keeps the commandment shall not come to harm.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: Vanity is named in the burial and forgetting of the wicked, and in the case where the righteous and wicked receive each other's due. The narrator calls each of these also vanity.

l: mirth and pleasure, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: The narrator commends mirth, since a man has nothing better under the sun than to eat, drink, and be joyful. This will accompany him in his labor all the days of the life God has given him.

l: work of God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: The narrator saw that man cannot find out the work of God that is done under the sun. Even a wise man who claims he can comprehend it will not find it, however much he labors.

l: the Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 8
s: The narrator urges keeping the king's command and reports what he has seen and applied his mind to under the sun. He commends mirth, labels certain outcomes vanity, and concludes after applying his heart to wisdom that the work of God cannot be found out.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: In Chapter 9 the narrator reflects that the righteous, the wise and their works are in God's hand, and that one event, death, comes alike to the righteous and the wicked, the clean and unclean, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. He argues that the living have hope, since a living dog is better than a dead lion, while the dead know nothing, have no reward and are forgotten. He urges people to eat, drink, wear white, enjoy life with the wife they love, and work with all their might, because there is no work or knowledge in Sheol. He observes that the race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong, since time and chance happen to all and no one knows his time. He closes with the story of a little city saved by a poor wise man whom no one remembered, concluding that wisdom is better than strength and weapons of war, though one sinner destroys much good.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The righteous, the wise and their works are said to be in God's hand, though man does not know whether love or hatred awaits him. God is also said to have already accepted the works of the one who enjoys his bread and wine, and he is the one who has given man his days of vanity under the sun.

l: the righteous, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The righteous, together with the wise and their works, are in the hand of God. They share the same event as the wicked, as the good do as the sinner, and the narrator counts this an evil under the sun.

l: the sinner, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The wicked meet the same event as the righteous, and the sinner fares as the good do. The narrator notes that the hearts of men are full of evil and madness while they live, and that one sinner destroys much good.

l: man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: Man does not know whether love or hatred awaits him, nor does he know his time. He is compared to fish caught in an evil net and birds caught in a snare, snared suddenly by an evil time.

l: the living, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The living have hope because they are joined with all the living, and a living dog is better than a dead lion. They know that they will die, and they are urged to enjoy their bread, wine, garments, wife and labor.

l: the dead, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The dead know nothing and have no further reward, and their memory is forgotten. Their love, hatred and envy have long perished, and they have no portion in anything done under the sun.

l: death, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: Death is the one event that comes to all alike, righteous and wicked, clean and unclean. After it people go to the dead, to Sheol, where there is no work, plan, knowledge or wisdom.

l: enjoyment of life, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The narrator urges people to eat their bread with joy, drink wine with a merry heart, keep their garments white and their heads anointed with oil. He also urges them to live joyfully with the wife they love, since this is their portion in life and labor, and to do whatever their hand finds with all their might.

l: time and chance, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: Time and chance happen to all, so that the race is not to the swift, the battle to the strong, bread to the wise, riches to the understanding, or favor to the skillful. Man does not know his time, and an evil time falls suddenly on people.

l: wisdom, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: Wisdom is said to be better than strength and better than weapons of war, and the words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of a ruler among fools. Yet the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard, and one sinner can destroy much good.

l: little city, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The little city had few men within it and was besieged by a great king who built great bulwarks against it. It was delivered by the wisdom of a poor wise man found in it.

l: great king, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: A great king came against the little city, besieged it and built great bulwarks against it. The city was nevertheless delivered by the poor wise man.

l: poor wise man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The poor wise man was found in the little city and delivered it by his wisdom. No one remembered him afterward, and his wisdom is despised and his words are not heard.

l: the Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 9
s: The narrator lays all this to heart to explore it, and concludes that one event comes to all and that time and chance govern outcomes. He returns to observe life under the sun, recounts a case of wisdom that seemed great to him, and affirms that wisdom is better than strength.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 10
s: Chapter 10 collects proverbs contrasting wisdom and folly. A little folly spoils wisdom and honor like dead flies in perfumer's oil, and the fool's speech begins in foolishness and ends in mischievous madness. The speaker describes an evil under the sun in which folly is given high dignity, the rich sit low, and servants ride horses while princes walk. The chapter warns that ordinary labors such as digging, quarrying, and splitting wood carry risks, and that skill brings success. It then contrasts a land whose king is a child and whose princes feast in the morning with one whose king is of noble birth, and ends by warning against slothfulness and against cursing the king or the rich, even privately.

l: the wise, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 10
s: The wise man's heart is at his right hand, and the words of his mouth are gracious. His wisdom and honor can be outweighed by a little folly, and skill is said to bring success.

l: fool, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 10
s: The fool's heart is at his left hand, and when he walks by the way his understanding fails him and he tells everyone he is a fool. His speech begins in foolishness and ends in mischievous madness, he multiplies words, and he is swallowed by his own lips. His labor wearies him because he doesn't know how to go to the city.

l: ruler, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 10
s: The ruler's spirit may rise up against a person, who is advised not to leave his place, since gentleness lays great offenses to rest. The speaker has seen an evil under the sun, a sort of error that proceeds from the ruler, in which folly is set in great dignity and the rich sit in a low place.

l: king, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 10
s: A land is called woeful when its king is a child and its princes eat in the morning, and happy when its king is the son of nobles and its princes eat in due season, for strength and not drunkenness. The text warns against cursing the king, even in one's thoughts, because a bird of the sky may carry the voice and tell the matter.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
s: Chapter 11 advises generous giving and diligent work despite not knowing what the future holds. The speaker urges casting bread on the waters and giving portions to seven or eight, since no one knows what evil may come on the earth. He says that one who watches the wind or clouds will neither sow nor reap, and that people cannot know the way of the wind, the growth of a child in the womb, or the work of God who does all. He therefore tells people to sow seed morning and evening, because they do not know which will prosper. The chapter ends by calling the light sweet and urging the young man to rejoice in his youth while remembering that God will bring him into judgment and that youth and the dawn of life are vanity.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
s: God is described as the one who does all, and his work is something people cannot know. He is also the one who will bring the young man into judgment for all his ways.

l: young man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
s: The young man is told to rejoice in his youth, let his heart cheer him, and walk in the ways of his heart and the sight of his eyes. He is warned that God will bring him into judgment for all these things, and is urged to remove sorrow from his heart and put away evil from his flesh.

l: generosity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
s: The unit urges casting bread on the waters, with the promise that it will be found after many days. It also advises giving a portion to seven, even to eight, because no one knows what evil will be on the earth.

l: uncertainty of the future, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
