s: People do not know what evil will come on the earth, the way of the wind, how bones grow in the womb, or the work of God. They also do not know which sowing will prosper, whether this or that or both. The unit also says that days of darkness will be many.

l: sowing and reaping, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
s: The one who observes the wind will not sow, and the one who regards the clouds will not reap. The reader is told to sow seed in the morning and not withhold the hand in the evening, since it is unknown which will prosper or whether both will be equally good.

l: judgment, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
s: The unit states that God will bring the young man into judgment for all the things he does in following his heart and eyes. This is given as the counterweight to the call to rejoice in youth.

l: youth, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
s: Youth is presented as a time to rejoice, with a cheerful heart and walking in the ways of the heart and the sight of the eyes. The unit also says that youth and the dawn of life are vanity, and that sorrow and evil should be removed.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 11
s: The unit says that all that comes is vanity, in the context of a man living many years and remembering the many days of darkness. It also calls youth and the dawn of life vanity.

l: Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: Chapter 12 closes the book by urging the reader to remember their Creator in youth, before the evil days of old age arrive. Old age and death are described through imagery of darkening lights, trembling keepers of the house, bowed strong men, failing desire, a severed silver cord and a broken golden bowl, after which the dust returns to the earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it. The Preacher declares 'Vanity of vanities! All is vanity!' and is described as a wise man who taught the people knowledge, pondered, sought out and set in order many proverbs, and sought acceptable words of truth. The words of the wise are compared to goads and well-fastened nails given from one shepherd, and the reader, addressed as 'my son', is warned that making many books has no end and much study wearies the flesh. The conclusion is to fear God and keep his commandments as the whole duty of man, for God will bring every work and hidden thing into judgment, whether good or evil.

l: God, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: God is named as the Creator whom the reader is told to remember in youth, and as the one who gave the spirit, to which it returns at death. He is the one to be feared, and he will bring every work, including every hidden thing, into judgment, whether good or evil.

l: the Preacher, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: The Preacher declares 'Vanity of vanities! All is vanity!' He is described as wise, still teaching the people knowledge, and pondering, seeking out and setting in order many proverbs. He sought to find acceptable words and words of truth written blamelessly.

l: old age and death, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: Old age is portrayed as the 'evil days' of fading pleasure, with trembling keepers of the house, bowed strong men, few grinders, darkened windows, shut doors, fear of heights, a burdensome grasshopper and failing desire. Death comes when the silver cord is severed and the golden bowl broken, as man goes to his everlasting home with mourners in the streets, the dust returning to the earth and the spirit to God.

l: youth, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: Youth is the time in which the reader is told to remember their Creator, before the evil days come and the years draw near when they will say they have no pleasure in them.

l: man, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: Man is said to go to his everlasting home, with mourners going about the streets, and his dust returns to the earth while his spirit returns to God. The whole duty of man is to fear God and keep his commandments, and every work and hidden thing of his will be judged.

l: vanity, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: Vanity is the Preacher's verdict on everything: 'Vanity of vanities! All is vanity!' It is stated in the passage after the description of aging and death.

l: God's commandments, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: God's commandments are to be kept, and doing so, together with fearing God, is called the end of the matter and the whole duty of man.

l: divine judgment, Ecclesiastes or, The Preacher, Chapter 12
s: God will bring every work into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil. This is given as the reason for fearing God and keeping his commandments.

l: The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon / Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 of the Song of Solomon opens as a song attributed to Solomon, in which the Beloved, a woman, longs for her lover's kisses and praises his love as better than wine. She describes herself as dark but lovely, explaining that the sun scorched her and that her mother's sons made her keeper of the vineyards, so she has not kept her own. She asks where her lover grazes his flock, and the Lover answers by telling her to follow the sheep's tracks, then compares her to a steed in Pharaoh's chariots. Friends, who speak as a group, promise to make her earrings of gold with studs of silver and say they will rejoice in the king. The Beloved and Lover then exchange praise, calling each other beautiful and describing their shared couch and the cedar and fir of their house.

l: Beloved, The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon / Chapter 1
s: The Beloved asks to be kissed, says his love is better than wine, and asks to be taken away, saying the king has brought her into his rooms. She calls herself dark but lovely, like Kedar's tents and Solomon's curtains, and says the sun scorched her and her mother's sons made her keeper of the vineyards while she did not keep her own. She asks where her lover grazes his flock, likens him to a sachet of myrrh and a cluster of henna blossoms from En Gedi, and calls him beautiful with a verdant couch.

l: Lover, The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon / Chapter 1
s: The Lover answers the Beloved's question by telling her to follow the sheep's tracks and graze her young goats beside the shepherds' tents. He compares her to a steed in Pharaoh's chariots and praises her cheeks and neck with their earrings and jewels. He calls her beautiful twice, says her eyes are like doves, and speaks of the house beams of cedar and rafters of fir.

l: love, The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon / Chapter 1
s: Love is described as better than wine, both by the Beloved speaking of her lover's love and by the Friends who say they will praise it more than wine. The virgins love the lover because his name is like oil poured out, and the Beloved says they are right to love him. The Beloved addresses him as the one whom her soul loves, and the Lover calls her "my love."

l: The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 is an exchange between a Lover and a Beloved. The speaker calls herself a rose of Sharon and a lily of the valleys, and describes sitting in her beloved's shadow, being brought to the banquet hall, and being faint with love. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires. She then relates how her beloved came leaping over the mountains and called her to rise and come away because winter is past and spring has arrived. The chapter closes with the call to catch the little foxes that plunder the vineyards, the declaration that the beloved is hers and she is his, and a plea that he turn and be like a roe or young deer on the mountains of Bether until the day is cool.

l: Lover, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: The Lover speaks at the start of the chapter, calling herself a rose of Sharon and a lily of the valleys, and she is faint with love. She relays the beloved's call to rise and come away because winter is past and the flowers, figs and vines are appearing. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires.

l: Beloved, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: The Beloved is described as like an apple tree among the trees of the wood, and as a roe or young deer who leaps on the mountains and stands behind the wall, looking through the windows and lattice. He speaks, calling his love, his beautiful one, to come away, and asks to see her face and hear her voice. He calls for the little foxes that plunder the blossoming vineyards to be caught, and is said to browse among the lilies.

l: love, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: Love is the banner over the speaker at the banquet hall, and she is faint with it. It is to be neither stirred up nor awakened until it so desires, as she charges the daughters of Jerusalem. Mutual belonging is stated in the line 'My beloved is mine, and I am his.'

l: The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3, the speaker describes seeking the one whom her soul loves at night on her bed and not finding him. She rises to search the city's streets and squares, is met by the watchmen, and soon finds him, holding him until she brings him to her mother's house. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires. A procession then comes up from the wilderness, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, and is identified as Solomon's carriage, guarded by sixty mighty men of Israel armed with swords. The chapter closes with a description of the carriage's silver, gold, and purple materials and a call to the daughters of Zion to see King Solomon crowned by his mother on his wedding day.

l: the beloved (him whom my soul loves), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: He is sought by the speaker at night on her bed, but she does not find him. After she passes the watchmen she finds him, and she holds him and will not let him go until she brings him into her mother's house, into the room of her who conceived her.

l: the speaker (narrator, 'my soul'), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: She seeks the one her soul loves at night, rises to search the city's streets and squares, and asks the watchmen if they have seen him. Having found him, she holds him and brings him to her mother's house. She then adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires.

l: daughters of Jerusalem, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: They are adjured by the speaker, by the roes and hinds of the field, not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires. They are also named as those from whom the middle of Solomon's carriage is paved with love.

l: love, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: Love is the subject of the speaker's charge, that it not be stirred up or awakened until it so desires. It is also said to pave the middle of Solomon's carriage, coming from the daughters of Jerusalem.

l: Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: Solomon is named as the owner of the carriage that comes up from the wilderness. King Solomon made the carriage for himself of Lebanon wood, silver, gold, and purple. The daughters of Zion are told to go out and see him wearing the crown with which his mother crowned him on his wedding day, the day of the gladness of his heart.

l: carriage (Solomon's carriage), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: The carriage is seen coming up from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh, frankincense, and all the spices of the merchant. King Solomon made it of the wood of Lebanon, with pillars of silver, a bottom of gold, and a seat of purple. Its middle is paved with love, from the daughters of Jerusalem, and sixty mighty men surround it.

l: mighty men of Israel (guards around Solomon's carriage), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: Sixty mighty men of Israel surround Solomon's carriage. They all handle the sword and are expert in war. Each has his sword on his thigh because of fear in the night.

l: Solomon's wedding day, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: It is described as the day of Solomon's weddings and the day of the gladness of his heart. On it King Solomon wears the crown with which his mother has crowned him, and the daughters of Zion are called to go out and see him.

l: The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: In Chapter 4, the lover praises his beloved, whom he calls his love, sister, and bride, describing her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, temples, neck, and breasts through images of doves, goats, shorn sheep, scarlet thread, pomegranate, David's tower, and fawns. He declares there is no spot in her and says he will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense until the day is cool. He calls her to come with him from Lebanon, from the peaks of Amana, Senir, and Hermon, and says she has ravished his heart and that her love is better than wine. He likens her to a locked garden, sealed fountain, and orchard of spices and precious fruits. At the end she calls on the north and south winds to blow on her garden so that her beloved may come into it and taste its fruits.

l: beloved (the bride's lover), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: She is praised as beautiful, with eyes like doves, hair like a flock of goats, teeth like shorn sheep, lips like scarlet thread, and a neck like David's tower. She is told there is no spot in her, is called to come away from Lebanon, and is said to have ravished the speaker's heart. At the end she invites the winds to blow on her garden and asks that her beloved come and taste its fruits.

l: Lover, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: He praises his beloved at length, calling her love, sister, and bride, and says she has ravished his heart with one of her eyes and one chain of her neck. He says he will go to the mountain of myrrh and hill of frankincense until the day is cool, and he calls her to come with him from Lebanon. He says her love is better than wine and her garments smell like Lebanon.

l: garden (the Beloved's garden), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: The bride is described as a locked up garden, a locked up spring, and a sealed fountain. Her shoots are called an orchard of pomegranates with precious fruits and spices such as henna, spikenard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, myrrh, and aloes, and she is a fountain of gardens and a well of living waters. In the final verse she calls the north and south winds to blow on it so its spices flow out, and asks that her beloved come into his garden and taste its fruits.

l: The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: In Chapter 5 the beloved declares he has come into his garden to gather myrrh, spice, honeycomb, honey, wine and milk, and friends urge him to eat and drink abundantly. The bride recounts that while she slept, her heart awake, her beloved knocked and asked her to open, but she hesitated over her robe and washed feet. When she rose to open, her hands dripping with myrrh, he had gone and did not answer her calls, and the watchmen of the city beat and bruised her and took her cloak. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is faint with love if they find him. When they ask how her beloved is better than others, she describes him from head to legs, as white and ruddy, golden-headed, and altogether lovely, her beloved and her friend.

l: daughters of Jerusalem, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: The daughters of Jerusalem are adjured by the bride to tell her beloved, should they find him, that she is faint with love. They respond by asking how her beloved is better than any other, prompting her extended description of him.

l: The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 opens with others asking the Beloved where her beloved has gone so they can seek him with her. She answers that he has gone down to his garden to pasture his flock and gather lilies, and she declares that she is his and he is hers. The Lover then praises her as beautiful as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, and awesome as an army with banners, describing her hair, teeth, and temples. He contrasts the sixty queens, eighty concubines, and countless virgins with his unique dove, whom her mother favored and whom the daughters, queens, and concubines praised. A speaker recounts going down to the nut tree grove and being carried among royal chariots, and Friends call on the Shulammite to return so they may gaze at her, to which the Lover responds by asking why they wish to gaze at her.

l: Beloved, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: The Beloved is asked where her beloved has gone and answers that he has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture his flock and gather lilies. She declares that she is her beloved's and he is hers. She is praised by the Lover as beautiful as Tirzah and awesome as an army with banners, and is called unique, her mother's only daughter, and blessed by the daughters, queens, and concubines.

l: Lover, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: The Lover praises his love as beautiful as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, and awesome as an army with banners, saying her eyes have overcome him. He compares her hair to a flock of goats, her teeth to ewes from the washing, and her temples to a piece of pomegranate. He sets the sixty queens, eighty concubines, and countless virgins against his dove, his perfect one, who is unique. At the end he asks why the friends desire to gaze at the Shulammite.

l: Shulammite, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: The Shulammite is called on by Friends to return, return so that they may gaze at her. The Lover responds by asking why they desire to gaze at her, as at the dance of Mahanaim.

l: The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: Chapter 7 is a speech of admiration addressed to a woman called the prince's daughter. The speaker praises her feet, thighs, body, waist, breasts, neck, eyes, nose, head and hair with a series of comparisons, and says the king is held captive in her tresses. He likens her stature to a palm tree and says he will climb it and take hold of its fruit. Her mouth is compared to the best wine that goes down smoothly for the beloved. The speaker then shifts, declaring that she belongs to her beloved and that his desire is toward her, and invites him to go out to the fields and villages and to the vineyards, where she will give him her love and where fruits stored up for him are at the doors.

l: prince's daughter, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: The prince's daughter is addressed and praised in detail, with her feet in sandals, thighs, body, waist, breasts, neck, eyes, nose, head and hair each compared to something, such as jewels, a goblet, wheat, fawns, towers, pools and Carmel. Her hair is said to hold the king captive in its tresses, and her stature is likened to a palm tree. She is called beautiful and pleasant, and her mouth is compared to the best wine.

l: beloved (the speaker's beloved), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: The beloved is the one to whom the woman declares she belongs, saying that his desire is toward her. She invites him to go out to the field, lodge in the villages and go early to the vineyards, where she will give him her love. She says that precious fruits, new and old, are at their doors, stored up for him.

l: The Song of Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: In Chapter 8, the Beloved wishes the Lover were like her brother so she could kiss him openly, and she imagines leading him to her mother's house and having him embrace her. She adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love before it desires, and Friends ask who is coming up from the wilderness leaning on her beloved. The Beloved asks to be set as a seal on his heart and arm, declaring that love is as strong as death and cannot be quenched by many waters. The Brothers speak of their little sister with no breasts and plan to build a silver turret or enclose her in cedar, and the Beloved answers that she is a wall with breasts like towers. She contrasts Solomon's leased vineyard at Baal Hamon with her own vineyard, and the chapter ends with the Lover being called to hear her voice and the Beloved urging him to come away like a gazelle on the mountains of spices.

l: Beloved, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: The Beloved wishes the Lover were like her brother so she could kiss him in public without scorn, and she imagines leading him to her mother's house and giving him spiced wine. She asks to be set as a seal on his heart and arm, and says she is a wall with breasts like towers who was in his eyes like one who found peace. She says her own vineyard is before her, gives the thousand to Solomon, and ends by urging her beloved to come away like a gazelle or young stag on the mountains of spices.

l: Lover, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: The Lover is the one the Beloved wishes to kiss and to lead into her mother's house, and he is pictured with his left hand under her head and his right embracing her. He is the beloved on whom she leans as she comes up from the wilderness. He is addressed as one who dwells in the gardens with friends in attendance, and is asked to let her hear his voice.

l: love, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: Love is described as strong as death, with jealousy as cruel as Sheol and flashes like fire, a very flame of the LORD. Many waters cannot quench it nor floods drown it, and a man who offered all the wealth of his house for it would be utterly scorned. The daughters of Jerusalem are adjured not to stir up or awaken it until it so desires.

l: Solomon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: Solomon had a vineyard at Baal Hamon, which he leased out to keepers who each had to bring a thousand shekels of silver for its fruit. The Beloved addresses him, saying the thousand are for him while two hundred go to those who tend the fruit of her own vineyard.

l: Solomon's vineyard at Baal Hamon, The Song of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: The vineyard at Baal Hamon belonged to Solomon and was leased out to keepers. Each keeper was to bring a thousand shekels of silver for its fruit.

l: vineyard (the Beloved's own), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: The Beloved's own vineyard is said to be before her, in contrast to Solomon's leased vineyard. She says the thousand are for Solomon and two hundred are for those who tend its fruit.

l: little sister (of the brothers), The Song of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: The Brothers speak of a little sister who has no breasts and ask what to do for her on the day she is spoken for. They say that if she is a wall they will build a turret of silver on her, and if she is a door they will enclose her with boards of cedar.

l: Baruch, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: Baruch, son of Nerias, wrote a book in Babylon in the fifth year, at the time the Chaldeans took and burned Jerusalem, and read it aloud to Jechonias king of Judah and to the assembled exiles by the river Sud. The people wept, fasted, prayed, and collected money according to each one's ability, sending it to Joakim the high priest and the priests in Jerusalem. The money was to buy burnt offerings, sin offerings, and incense, and the exiles asked for prayers for the lives of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon and his son Baltasar, and for themselves. They instructed that the book be read in the house of the Lord on feast days and assembly days as a confession that righteousness belongs to the Lord and confusion of face to Judah. The confession recounts that the people, kings, princes, priests, prophets, and fathers disobeyed the Lord from the exodus from Egypt onward, ignored the prophets, and so suffered plagues and the curse declared through Moses.

l: Baruch, Baruch, Baruch / Chapter 1
s: Baruch, son of Nerias, wrote the book in Babylon in the fifth year, when the Chaldeans took and burned Jerusalem. He read its words in the hearing of Jechonias, the elders, the mighty men, and all the people living at Babylon by the river Sud.
